forces.title: Policy uncertainty and fiscal changes deter UK energy investment
forces.description: The UK's current fiscal and regulatory regimes, particularly the Energy Profits Levy (EPL), are hampering investment in domestic oil and gas. Policy uncertainty and frequent changes have led to a projected halving of capital investment by 2028, causing capital flight and skilled workers to move abroad. This undermines energy security and foregoes a potential £50 billion private capital investment opportunity.

forces.title: Fiscal reform offers £50 billion private capital injection for energy
forces.description: OEUK modelling shows that reforming the Energy Profits Levy (EPL) to the Oil and Gas Revenue Levy (OGRL) from 2027 could unlock £50 billion in private capital investment for 111 additional UK energy projects. This would provide a more predictable framework for investors, boost domestic energy production, and strengthen supply chain activity, significantly enhancing the UK's long-term energy security and economic value.

forces.title: Government infrastructure spending provides critical economic floor
forces.description: Government infrastructure spending in the UK is acting as a crucial economic floor, supporting GDP growth amidst weak private sector activity. This public investment provides a stable base for the broader infrastructure sector, offering resilience against broader economic uncertainties and high financing costs. This intervention is vital for maintaining project pipelines and overall market stability, especially for traditional infrastructure assets.
forces.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

forces.title: Contracts for Difference mechanism drives low-carbon infrastructure investment
forces.description: The Contracts for Difference (CfD) mechanism remains central to UK offshore wind deployment, effectively attracting private capital into low-carbon infrastructure. The expanded CfD budget (from £900 million to £1.8 billion) and extended CfD period (to 20 years) further strengthen investor interest. This policy support helps secure large capacities, such as the 8.4 GW awarded in Allocation Round 7, despite rising financing and supply chain costs.

forces.title: Higher financing costs and inflation strain infrastructure project viability
forces.description: Inflation, higher financing costs, and supply chain pressures are significantly impacting the viability of infrastructure projects, particularly in offshore wind. These factors lead to higher strike prices required in mechanisms like CfD. For the broader construction sector, rising financing and construction costs are weakening project viability, contributing to subdued investment activity and increasing insolvency risks across firms of all sizes.

forces.title: Expanding definition of infrastructure assets for private investment
forces.description: The concept of "infrastructure" for private capital is rapidly expanding beyond traditional assets (roads, ports) to include new categories like data centers, charging stations, fiber-optic networks, digital infrastructure, infrastructure services, and social infrastructure (e.g., radiology chains). This broadening scope requires investors to develop new research capabilities and adapt their investment strategies to embrace a wider array of asset classes, each with varying risk/return profiles.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Strong LP interest boosts infrastructure asset class allocations
forces.description: Limited partners (LPs) show robust and increasing interest in infrastructure as an asset class, with 51% planning to raise allocations over the next three years. Infrastructure fundraising grew by 9% CAGR (2020-2025), outpacing other private market categories. This strong LP sentiment, driven by diversification and expected return improvements, indicates significant headroom for growth, even as high dry powder challenges deployment speed.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Infrastructure investment shifts up risk curve for higher returns
forces.description: To achieve higher returns in a maturing market, infrastructure investors are increasingly shifting capital from "traditional core" assets to "core plus" and "value added" strategies. These higher-risk approaches, which saw significant fundraising growth (core-plus up 390%), involve greater exposure to construction, demand, and operational risks. This cyclical pivot reflects investors' pursuit of enhanced performance beyond stable, lower-return assets.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Extended holding periods and declining liquidity pressure returns
forces.description: Infrastructure investments are experiencing lengthening capital cycles, with average holding periods extending to 7.6 years by 2025 and distributions to paid-in capital (DPI) declining to 13%. This reduction in liquidity, coupled with rising debt costs and elevated asset purchase prices, creates significant pressure on traditional IRR targets. Investors are increasingly challenged to generate returns in a competitive market with slower exits.
forces.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

forces.title: Shift from financial structuring to operational performance for value
forces.description: Return drivers in infrastructure investment are shifting away from multiple expansion and financial structuring towards active value creation through operational performance and capital productivity. Investors are increasingly focusing on improving the underlying business performance, acquiring stakes in earlier-stage greenfield/brownfield projects, and higher-complexity businesses. This demands enhanced managerial excellence and the ability to design and support complex operating models.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: AI-driven capital productivity enhances infrastructure project efficiency
forces.description: AI is emerging as a significant lever for capital productivity in infrastructure, enabling greater efficiency in project development and execution. AI-enabled generative scheduling tools can optimize sequencing to reduce build timelines and costs for capital-intensive projects. In renewables, AI supports the full greenfield cycle, from site identification to construction, enhancing capital efficiency and improving IRR.
forces.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

forces.title: Strained returns and declining EBITDA margins for private European infrastructure
forces.description: Returns from European infrastructure investments have been strained, with infrastructure stocks delivering significantly lower total shareholder returns (35% vs. Euronext 100's 82% from 2019-2025). Privately held assets experienced average EBITDA margin declines of two percentage points across most sub-asset classes between 2019 and 2023, with an average return on assets of only 3.5%. This indicates a challenging environment for generating strong financial performance.
forces.source_title: European infrastructure is evolving—and investors are, too

forces.title: Rise of Gen AI fuels demand for digital infrastructure investment
forces.description: The rapid rise of generative AI and the accelerating transition to cloud computing are significantly increasing computational loads, spurring substantial growth in demand for Europe's digital infrastructure. This trend creates a strong tailwind for investment in assets like data centers, fiber-optic networks, and other AI-adjacent infrastructure, driving new opportunities for capital deployment in this expanding segment of the infrastructure asset class.
forces.source_title: European infrastructure is evolving—and investors are, too

forces.title: AI tools enhance deal identification for infrastructure investors
forces.description: Leveraging AI tools for deal identification is becoming a critical differentiator for infrastructure investors seeking opportunities outside conventional pipelines. AI and large language models can analyze extensive data to improve the efficiency of origination processes, helping identify new targets and generate proprietary insights. This allows investors to focus on the most promising opportunities, enhancing competitive advantage in a crowded market.
forces.source_title: European infrastructure is evolving—and investors are, too

viewpoints.title: UK fiscal policy crucial for unlocking significant energy infrastructure investment
viewpoints.description: OEUK argues that a more competitive and predictable UK fiscal regime, specifically reforming the Energy Profits Levy (EPL) from 2027 to the Oil and Gas Revenue Levy (OGRL), is critical. This change could unlock an additional £50 billion in private capital investment across 111 projects, sustaining domestic energy production well into the 2030s. The current environment constrains future developments, threatening energy security and economic value.

viewpoints.title: CfD mechanism vital for attracting private capital into low-carbon infrastructure
viewpoints.description: OEUK highlights the Contracts for Difference (CfD) mechanism's central role in UK offshore wind deployment, reaffirming its importance in attracting private capital to low-carbon infrastructure. Allocation Round 7 (AR7) secured a record 8.4 GW capacity, demonstrating continued investor confidence. However, the sector faces challenges from higher financing costs and supply chain pressures, necessitating focus on improving competitiveness beyond just auction volumes.

viewpoints.title: Digital infrastructure investment requires asset-specific due diligence for value
viewpoints.description: BCG advises that the expanding digital infrastructure asset class, driven by AI, demands a refined investor approach. Broad exposure is risky; value accrues from asset-level portfolio choices. Investors must adopt fundamental due diligence, understand technology trends, and adapt underwriting frameworks. Costs of misclassification are rising, with assets exhibiting diverging economic behaviors, impacting valuations and exit timelines for execution-heavy assets like B2C fiber.
viewpoints.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

viewpoints.title: Asset-heavy NetCos yield weak returns, prompting portfolio re-composition
viewpoints.description: BCG's 2026 Telco Value Creators Report indicates that asset-heavy NetCos spun out from operating businesses delivered a negative five-year total shareholder return (-4%), the weakest among telco archetypes. This, coupled with capital-intensive 5G and FTTH rollouts failing to significantly boost ARPU, signals pressure on operators. They must decompose portfolios, reposition ownership through partnerships/JVs, repurpose assets, and adopt AI-first operations for value creation.
viewpoints.source_title: The Digital Infrastructure Universe Continues to Expand. Here's How to Benefit.

viewpoints.title: Government spending props up UK infrastructure, private activity lags
viewpoints.description: Allianz Trade reports that UK GDP growth remains sluggish but resilient, with government infrastructure spending providing a crucial floor. However, private sector activity continues to be weak. This suggests a mixed outlook for infrastructure investment, where public funds are critical for stability but private capital deployment faces headwinds amid broader economic uncertainties and higher financing costs.
viewpoints.source_title: Q3 UK economic outlook: Growth holds, inflation bites

viewpoints.title: Private capital crucial to meet rising global infrastructure investment needs
viewpoints.description: McKinsey highlights an imperative for $106 trillion in global infrastructure investments by 2040, encompassing traditional and next-generation assets like data centers and fiber networks. Public sector funding alone is insufficient, making private capital increasingly vital. Global infrastructure fundraising reached a record $200 billion in 2025, with limited partners (LPs) planning to increase allocations, reinforcing infrastructure's position as a leading asset class for private investment.
viewpoints.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

viewpoints.title: Infrastructure investment shifts to value-added for higher returns
viewpoints.description: As the infrastructure sector matures, investors are increasingly moving up the risk curve from "traditional core" to "core plus" and "value added" strategies to pursue higher returns. The majority of 2025 infrastructure fundraising occurred in these higher-risk categories, with core-plus growing significantly. This shift reflects investor demand for better performance, although such strategies entail greater exposure to construction, demand, and operational risks.
viewpoints.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

viewpoints.title: Declining liquidity and extended holding periods challenge infrastructure returns
viewpoints.description: Infrastructure investments are experiencing lengthening capital cycles, with holding periods extending and distributions to paid-in capital (DPI) declining to 13% by 2025. Traditional internal rate of return (IRR) targets face pressure from higher debt costs and elevated asset purchase prices. This necessitates a shift from passive investment to active value creation, with a focus on operational performance and capital productivity to generate alpha in a maturing, competitive market.
viewpoints.source_title: Infrastructure: Investing to support global growth

viewpoints.title: European infrastructure asset class growing but strained returns and high dry powder
viewpoints.description: European infrastructure's AUM grew to €487 billion in 2025 with a 16.5% CAGR since 2014, driven by energy transition and macro tailwinds. However, returns have been strained, particularly between 2019-2025 (35% TSR vs. 82% Euronext 100 benchmark), and EBITDA margins for privately held assets have declined. This has led to high levels of dry powder (€789 billion in Europe by 2024) as capital deployment slows despite strong LP sentiment.
viewpoints.source_title: European infrastructure is evolving—and investors are, too

viewpoints.title: Broadening asset scope and AI leverage critical for European infrastructure investment
viewpoints.description: McKinsey advises European infrastructure investors to think creatively to deploy dry powder and achieve adequate returns in a competitive environment. This involves building strong research capabilities in new subsectors (beyond traditional assets), leveraging AI tools for deal identification to surface opportunities outside typical pipelines, and enhancing value creation at the due diligence stage. This strategy is crucial as the scope of infrastructure assets expands significantly.
viewpoints.source_title: European infrastructure is evolving—and investors are, too

Policy mechanisms like Allocation Round 7 (AR7) provide crucial support, awarding contracts and attracting private capital to low-carbon infrastructure projects.

Capital is allocated to developing green hydrogen infrastructure, supporting its role as a key energy vector in the transition.
